title: The Biological Clock-Mitochondria Axis in the Liver: From Molecular Mechanisms to Metabolic Disease
content: The liver ranks among the peripheral organs exhibiting the most robust circadian rhythmicity, with glucose homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and bile acid turnover governed by tightly phased diurnal oscillations. Mitochondria are the primary executors of these metabolic programs, their functional output temporally coordinated with the circadian state of the hepatocyte. Accumulating evidence indicates that the mitochondrial network undergoes dynamic remodeling throughout the 24-hour cycle, encompassing oscillatory changes in bioenergetics, fusion–fission balance, and quality control. This clock–mitochondria interplay is bidirectional: core clock components drive rhythmic remodeling via CDK1/MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of DRP1 and the NAD⁺–SIRT1/SIRT3 axis, while retrograde mitochondrial signals -including ROS flux and acetyl-CoA availability-modulate clock amplitude and entrainment. Disruption of this temporal architecture promotes metabolic dysfunction underlying MASLD onset and progression to MASH and HCC. As the clock–mitochondria axis operates upstream of these pathogenic cascades, its chronopharmacological restoration constitutes a mechanistically grounded therapeutic strategy. Interventions including time-restricted feeding, NAD⁺ precursor supplementation, PPAR agonists, and ACC inhibitors converge on clock-regulated mitochondrial pathways and may yield enhanced efficacy when delivered in a circadian-informed manner. This review delineates the molecular architecture of hepatic clock–mitochondria coupling, its breakdown across the MASLD/MASH continuum, and the translational rationale for mitochondria-centered chronotherapy.
